title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in first-of-its kind IPO
description: Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation t
body: Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble."Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market."There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available."We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."   The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product"."AI carries real risks," she added.Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

schema.headline: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in first-of-its kind IPO

title: Senegal boat disaster: Dozens missing as migrant boat sinks
description: Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat said to be carrying between 50 and 100 migrants capsized in the Atlantic Ocean.Fo
body: Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat said to be carrying between 50 and 100 migrants capsized in the Atlantic Ocean.Four bodies have reportedly been recovered so far. Dozens of people are still missing.Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT)."Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.However, a local official told Reuters news agency it was carrying 50 people, adding that the boat hit a rock as migrants were transferring from small fishing boats to a larger vessel.Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.The Senegalese navy said it had rescued more than 1,400 people on Monday and Tuesday this week.As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary Islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.It said more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.

schema.headline: Senegal boat disaster: Dozens missing as migrant boat sinks

title: Bududa landslide: Ugandan survivors  seek justice at the UN
description: ByOndiro Oganga and Swaibu IbrahimBBC AfricaReporting fromKampalaSurvivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have
body: ByOndiro Oganga and Swaibu IbrahimBBC AfricaReporting fromKampalaSurvivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking  climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.At least 33 of the 53 people who died in the 2019 landslide were children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family."My quest should be a lesson," he said. "Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens." Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.Last month, it launched a new resettlement programme offering affected households 18m Ugandan shillings ($4,300; £3,300) to help them move to safer areas.But some survivors have questioned whether the amount is enough to cover the cost of relocating and rebuilding their lives.Under the programme, families can choose between receiving two acres of land, valued at 8m shillings, plus 10m shillings  towards building a house, or taking the equivalent land allowance in cash, alongside the same housing grant.The scheme is expected to benefit 1,410 households identified as living in high-risk areas.The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods."I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.They are seeking compensation for lost family members and livelihoods, as well as emergency measures, including accessible early-warning systems in high-risk areas.Greenwatch Executive Director Samantha Atukunda Kakuru Mwesigwa said the case is about changing how governments prepare and respond to climate-related disasters."Justice for claimants is not just about winning in court. It is about forcing government policy to keep pace with a changing climate, and ensuring loss and damage is no longer an afterthought in disaster management," she said.The threat of climate-related disasters extends across East Africa.In Kenya, floods and landslides killed at least 181 people between March and May 2024, according to the Kenya Red Cross. In Rwanda, floods and landslides killed 135 people in May 2023.The dangers are also being felt further afield. In October 2026, a flash flood swept through Nepal's Gorkha district after a landslide blocked a river, washing away homes and infrastructure, and killing over 1,500 people."Disasters like the one in Bududa are only getting worse because of climate change – and they are happening all around the world, as we've seen recently and tragically in Nepal," ClientEarth lawyer Vesselina Newman said.She said poorer countries, which have contributed relatively little to global  emissions, are bearing some of the heaviest consequences of climate change and need greater financial support."High income countries must provide financial assistance and ensure that sufficient money goes directly to countries like Uganda, so they can roll out life-saving adaptation measures," she said.The complainants say relocation must involve more than moving people out of danger.They want the government to protect their livelihoods, respect their land rights, and take account of individual needs.The case is now before the United Nations Human Rights Committee, which will ask the Ugandan government to respond within six months.More Uganda stories on BBC:

schema.headline: Bududa landslide: Ugandan survivors  seek justice at the UN

title: Lahori Zeera, Campa Jeera: Cumin-laced fizzy sodas are giving the cola giants a tough fight in India
description: It began as an impromptu kitchen experiment.Saurabh Munjal, Nikhil Doda and Saurabh Bhutna - three cousins in India's north-western Punjab state - wer
body: It began as an impromptu kitchen experiment.Saurabh Munjal, Nikhil Doda and Saurabh Bhutna - three cousins in India's north-western Punjab state - were messing about at home post dinner one evening, when Doda casually brewed up a tangy cumin-flavoured fizzy soda using regular pantry ingredients.They enjoyed its earthy, piquant taste so much that they decided to explore options to sell it commercially.Cumin-laced sodas had always been sold at street-side stalls in India, but it was a broken market of local companies. Not many had built a carbonated beverage brand around the flavour.The trio persuaded their families to invest some capital and launched Lahori Zeera in 2017. Zeera is the Hindi name for cumin.Almost a decade on, the drink has become a bit of a sensation in India, challenging the entrenched monopoly of global cola giants, especially in the all-important mass-market ten-rupee ($0.11; £0.078) beverage category - it will close this year with revenues of $115-120m.Its popularity reflects a growing consumer preference for distinctly Indian flavours and drinks perceived to be more healthy, say analysts. Lahori Zeera is one of several cumin-flavoured soda brands that have mushroomed across the country over the past decade. There's Jeeru from Mumbai-based Xotik Frujus, Campa Jeera from billionaire Mukesh Ambani-owned Campa Cola and at least half-a-dozen other variants from regional players including Fizz Jeera Masala from House of Bindu. Bindu launched their cumin soda nearly 25 years ago, but sales were flat until some years ago, according to Megha Shankar, a director with the company."Now it is the fastest growing category among carbonated beverages," Shankar told the BBC. "Its contribution to our revenues has doubled from 20% to 40% in the last five years."Soaring demand for the product has pushed House of Bindu to widen its footprint across the country, after being largely based in southern India for over two decades. Parle Agro, external, one of India's oldest consumer brands, also rolled out its own cumin soda brand Dhishoom nationally last year after exclusively selling it in rural markets since 2012.Online orders for these fizzy drinks, meanwhile, were up 900% this summer according to a report from one of India's online delivery companies. The cumin frenzy is reshaping India's non-alcoholic beverages market, which was valued at $32 billion in 2024 and projected to double by 2033.According to a report from Kotak Mutual Fund earlier this year, Lahori Zeera, Campa and other smaller challengers - now dubbed as India's "ethnic beverages market" - collectively doubled their share of India's carbonated soft-drinks market to around 15% by September last year, while the combined market share of  Coca-Cola and PepsiCo fell from roughly 93% to 85%."This is a "Jio moment" for beverages. Just as telecom incumbents bled market share when data prices crashed, beverage incumbents are bleeding volume," the Kotak report said, drawing an analogy to the disruption caused by the entry of Reliance-owned Jio Telecom in India's telecoms market in 2016."In global markets, established duopolies rarely lose more than 1-2% share annually; an 8% swing in less than a year is a structural disruption."Saurabh Munjal, CEO of Archian Foods which manufactures Lahori Zeera, told the BBC that the company has "always been in a situation where we are sold out each year. We've doubled our capacity to 1.2 million bottles per day last year and are still unable to meet demand".For decades, the colas have had a dominant presence in India, appealing to the aspirational part of the population as lifestyle products that were cool to consume.With millions of dollars in marketing budgets splashed out on billboards, Bollywood stars and cricket championships, they sold a very western idea of hydration to India, says Munjal.But home-grown brands are now mounting a serious challenge with a combination of smart distribution, attractive pricing and a turn towards nostalgic Indian flavours such as cumin, raw mango, kokum fruit and tamarind.Munjal says that for long, there has been a tendency among consumer brands in India to either westernise Indian products or "Indianise" western products. But with Lahori Zeera, which uses the tagline "apna desi thanda", meaning India's own cold drink, his desire is to change that. Shankar says her brand has also recently launched a zero-sugar version of their cumin soda to capture the growing market for healthier non-cola drinks.This success notwithstanding, sustaining this winning trajectory will not be easy for these ethnic beverage brands, say analysts. The very factors that propelled their rise could also limit growth."The million-dollar question is how big can the cumin-flavoured drink market become. And I suspect it won't become as big as the colas," Rajiv Agarwal, a professor at Mumbai-based SP Jain Institute of Management, who advises family businesses on strategies to succeed against multi-national corporations, told the BBC.The 10-rupee price point, which accounts for the bulk of sales volumes in India's cumin-flavoured carbonated drinks market, is another double-edged sword.While it has driven up sales, the soaring cost of plastic, packaging, sugar and other raw material amid the global energy shock could start to hit margins, which are already very thin. Raising prices, meanwhile, could affect volumes, forcing brands to further reduce bottle sizes, something the cola companies had resorted to a few years ago. Then there is always the threat of bigger, deep-pocketed players coming in to disrupt the category."Competition is extremely aggressive," says Agarwal. And the established global players are better organised in terms of systems, processes, distribution channels and bottling arrangements.Coca Cola, which had acquired the cumin-flavoured Rimzim brand in the 1990s, is strengthening its play in this category and reportedly doubled production last year. But the challenges haven't deterred the ambitions of the homegrown players. "Indian flavours need to find a global spotlight," says Munjal, who is looking to tap the global market in the coming years."For generations, we've grown up drinking colas of the world, but I hope the next generations will drink the zeeras of India."Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external X, external and Facebook, external.

schema.headline: Lahori Zeera, Campa Jeera: Cumin-laced fizzy sodas are giving the cola giants a tough fight in India

title: Florida pastor found guilty over role in assassination of Haitian president
description: A Florida pastor has been found guilty of a number of charges relating to the assassination of the Haitian President Jovenel Moïse.Christian Emmanuel
body: A Florida pastor has been found guilty of a number of charges relating to the assassination of the Haitian President Jovenel Moïse.Christian Emmanuel Sanon, a dual US-Haitian national, was convicted of all eight charges against him, including conspiracy to kill or kidnap a person. He faces a potential sentence of life in prison.The 67-year-old was accused of being involved in a plot to replace Moïse as Haiti's president with himself in 2021, allegedly so he could award lucrative contracts to a Florida-based security outfit once in place.The murder of Moïse has left Haiti without a leader for five years. That political vacuum has intensified gang violence in the impoverished Caribbean nation.A presidential election is scheduled for next year and Moïse's wife, Martine, who was injured in the attack that killed her husband, announced this week that she intended to stand.Sanon was found guilty on Wednesday following an eight-week trial in federal court in Miami, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner. His lawyer said he maintains his innocence and that he intends to appeal against the verdict, it reports.Prosecutors said Sanon had "political aspirations" in Haiti and, in April 2021, met several other co-conspirators to devise a plan to oust Moïse in an armed raid on the presidential palace in the capital, Port-au-Prince.Among them were the heads of the companies Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security - collectively referred to as CTU - who would finance the coup in exchange for government contracts for infrastructure projects, and to provide security forces and equipment.A few months later, the other conspirators realised that Sanon had "neither the constitutional qualifications nor the popular support" to become Haiti's president and so shifted to another candidate, the US Department of Justice said.At the same time, the plot had developed from one to forcibly remove Moïse from office to assassinating him, investigators said.Dozens of people have been implicated in the conspiracy, which prosecutors said involved co-ordinating funding for and delivering weapons and mercenaries to Haiti to carry out the attack.  On 6 July that year, a group of Colombian mercenaries entered the presidential palace and killed Moïse. His wife, who was also injured in the attack, said at the time that the assailants had "riddled" her husband with bullets.The successful assassination plot raised questions in Haiti about the relative ease with which the mercenaries were able to gain access to the president.The country - the poorest in the Americas - has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but Moïse's assassination ushered in a period of worsening instability that emboldened gangs and prompted the deployment of a multinational force.However, this has struggled to penetrate areas where gangs hold sway and more than 5,700 people have been killed or injured in the year to 11 September, the UN said last month.Sanon and several other co-conspirators were arrested by Haitian authorities, while three mercenaries were killed in a gun battle with police. Eighteen people were transferred to Florida in September to stand trial over the plot.Four men, including the heads of the CTU, were convicted of their role earlier this year. Sanon had been scheduled to be tried with them, but his case was delayed due to health reasons, according to CBS.Sanon was born in Haiti but moved to the US as a teenager. He told the court he had worked in churches in Haitian immigrant communities in several parts of the US including Florida, US media report.

schema.headline: Florida pastor found guilty over role in assassination of Haitian president

title: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
description: US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following
body: US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.In the same post, the president announced  he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House. While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend". He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue."Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran.""We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon".Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine - but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.As the talks were under way in China, and even as Putin was holding his press conference claiming to be ready for peace, Ukraine's capital Kyiv was under attack from Russian drones.Putin has repeatedly rejected all ceasefire offers from Ukraine, insisting on his maximalist demands which Kyiv and its European allies say are tantamount to de facto capitulation of Ukraine. In Shenzhen, the Kremlin leader also vowed a "far more painful" retaliation in response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea. A missile and drone attack on Tuesday destroyed its central road section.There was no mention from Putin of almost five years of Russian attacks on power plants, bridges and residential buildings in Ukraine.The Russian president also directly addressed comparisons between his meeting with Trump and Xi and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the US met towards the end of World War Two."Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after WW2."And when it comes to today's conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted."The Kremlin released a video showing Putin leaving the summit venue and saying goodbye to Xi."Thank you for organising this," Putin said. "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."Meanwhile, China's president described his meeting with Putin and Trump as "positive, constructive, and highly productive", according to the country's state broadcaster CCTV.It added that Xi recalled "the history of fighting side-by-side during WW2", as the three leaders emphasised the importance of "cherishing the hard-won peace".Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Putin.Some Russian newspapers called it a "diplomatic victory" as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine many Western leaders were trying to isolate him.The summit also marked the first time since Russia's war in Ukraine began that Putin took part in an international gathering attended by leaders from countries including Canada, Japan and Australia.US lawmakers responded with frustration to Trump's warmth towards America's geopolitical adversaries."I was encouraged by some of the commitments that came out of the President's meetings in Asia, particularly the recognition that nuclear war must never be fought," Republican Senator John Curtis said in an emailed statement to the BBC.But Curtis also said he was concerned about Trump's approach to the foreign leaders, adding that "Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends"."We should not treat them as though they share our values or interests," Curtis, who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, added. "Doing so risks undermining our national security, weakening trust with our allies, and sending the wrong message about where America stands."Jeanne Shaheen, a ranking Democratic member on the same committee, chose harsher words in her comment. "President Trump's 'friend' is a murderous war criminal," she wrote on X.With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon

schema.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting

title: UK and EU to agree youth mobility scheme, BBC understands
description: Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agree
body: Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum. A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday."There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said."But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow."So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes. An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling. Burnham has also said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU. However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun, external, said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU. He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Thursday, Badenoch said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but "not trade at any cost". She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc. Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey told BBC Newsnight that while he agreed with Burnham on "the harms of Brexit", he did not think the prime minister was "going to go anywhere near far enough"."We need to go further and faster," he said, including returning to freedom of movement - which Sir Ed said would help tackle immigration and boost the UK economy.

schema.headline: UK and EU to agree youth mobility scheme, BBC understands

title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
description: European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv."Europe has
body: European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv."Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing. Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks"."That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable". Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition. Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions. Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine"."These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen."A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.He also sought to downplay the Shenzhen summit as above all "a photo opportunity." "The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase," Merz added.Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also took exception to Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, saying:  "Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be."Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine. It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory. As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not."I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.Kyiv and its European allies say that – in the absence of any major success on the vast front line – the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.

schema.headline: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

title: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
description: Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ord
body: Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile said that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he said.An image, meanwhile, showed six armoured vehicles, including tanks and bulldozers, around Salah al-Din road.A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter.""We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.Multiple verified videos of the aftermath of the incursion on Thursday showed destruction, earth banks, and heavy vehicle tracks more than 1.2km beyond the Yellow Line.That is believed to be the furthest Israeli troops have advanced into central Gaza since they occupied the so-called Netzarim Corridor before the ceasefire.Some residents returned to check their properties following the Israeli withdrawal."The entire area has been destroyed, and we honestly do not know what to do," Abd Aliwa told Reuters news agency as he sat beside a pile of rubble.Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second was killed to the north in Gaza City, and the third was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".Gaza health officials said another two people were killed on Thursday by Israeli fire in eastern Gaza City, according to Reuters. There was no immediate comment from the IDF.At least 1,662 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Since then, more than 74,710 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, its health ministry says.

schema.headline: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line

title: Elon Musk says record $446m spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
description: Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican def
body: Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive was the election's top individual donor, giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president. Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US. Musk was speaking virtually, external at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders."I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."This marks a major shift in tone by Musk, who has previously been seen wearing a Maga hat."I'm not just Maga, I'm dark, gothic Maga," he joked at a Trump rally in 2024.For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending. In October 2026, the Pentagon named Musk as a co-lead of a future of warfare study called Project Meridian, while he continued to travel with and advise Trump.Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings, as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.

schema.headline: Elon Musk says record $446m spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'

title: China's Xi Jinping has orchestrated a  remarkable diplomatic moment - but it comes with pitfalls
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are meeting for a historic trilateral summitByLaura BickerChina c
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are meeting for a historic trilateral summitByLaura BickerChina correspondent Reporting fromShenzhenXi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table. And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.  Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.Ukraine, the balancing actFirst, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year, to be on the agenda.This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's full-scale invasion.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Russia's invasion of Ukraine, now into its fifth year, has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives The US, especially under the previous Biden administration, and Europe have accused China of sending Russia components that it could use in its war in Ukraine, while also propping up the country's economy by buying oil and gas.Xi wants to keep Putin close, but not too close because he also doesn't want Russia's problems to become China's problems.China's growing nuclear arsenal Donald Trump has already made it clear he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting the world's supply of nuclear weapons. The US and Russia possess the world's largest stockpile of nuclear warheads. But China is rapidly expanding its own arsenal, which is raising alarm bells in Washington.The last major US-Russian arms control treaty, known as New START, expired in February this year, triggering fears of an arms race.  The agreement had set a cap to control the number of nuclear weapons in US and Russia's arsenal.Trump would like China to be included in any new agreement, but Beijing has pushed back.Xi's argument will be that his arsenal is considerably smaller than what Washington and Moscow own, and, therefore, it would be unfair for Beijing to be bound by their limits. China also believes it should have the freedom to develop its own nuclear capabilities.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, China unveiled intercontinental nuclear missiles at a military parade in 2025This subject could complicate Xi's bid for China to be recognised as a leader on the world stage - because the US could argue that the status includes being a responsible nuclear power.Will everyone stick to the script?Xi will want to control the optics of this meeting, from start to finish. Chinese officials like to nail down agendas with talking points and produce carefully choreographed speeches.But in this unprecedented summit, Xi will have to live with two very unpredictable leaders.Both Trump and Putin have their own agendas and the US President has already threatened to go off script.There is a risk that they both dominate the meeting and Xi ends up looking like a host, rather than the architect of a major diplomatic moment.Of course, Xi may be ready for this. It may even play into his hands.The Chinese leader has been trying to portray himself as a stable global leader - at this summit he will be flanked by two men embroiled in wars they cannot seem to end.So any unscripted moment could serve to highlight his preferred role as senior statesman.Xi's problems at homeFor all the attention, this meeting of three men with vastly different agendas is unlikely to yield any significant outcomes. But the power it projects is important for Xi as he heads towards next year's Communist Party Congress, where he is expected to secure a historic fourth term as leader of the party and country.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A job fair in Jiangsu province: China has been battling youth unemployment in a sluggish economy He may hope to use this as propaganda at home, given the country is grappling with huge domestic challenges.A country-wide property crisis has dented consumer confidence. Local governments are heavily in debt. Manufacturing has slowed and more of China's workforce has become dependent on flexible jobs with no pension or social security. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find work. Frustration and anxiety about the future bubble up routinely. Xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow.At a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a new era.

schema.headline: China's Xi Jinping has orchestrated a  remarkable diplomatic moment - but it comes with pitfalls

title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
description: Figure caption, Rohingya genocide: What was said in court and what happens now?ByAleks PhillipsAnna HolliganReporting fromat The Hague, and Jonathan H
body: Figure caption, Rohingya genocide: What was said in court and what happens now?ByAleks PhillipsAnna HolliganReporting fromat The Hague, and Jonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondentMyanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Rohingyas at the Cox's Bazar camp in Bangladesh, where around a million refugees now reside, watched the verdict liveThe court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen. The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.Figure caption, Watch: Genocide judgement will 'mean a great deal' for Rohingya communityIwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes. He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.'Recognition of our suffering'The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups."This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Rohingya refugees were seen reacting as the ICJ verdict was broadcast on a big screen in Cox's Bazar, BangladeshPhilippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment". He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings. He added that, while ruling against Myanmar did not mean the court would find similarly with Gaza, if it had not found Myanmar responsible, the case against Israel "would, in effect, be over". Israel says the case against it is "wholly unfounded".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, ICJ president Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya populationAntonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.A spokesperson for the US State Department said "the proper interpretation" of the Genocide Convention is of "paramount importance", and so is "preventing politicisation" of the International Criminal Court. "We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," they said.They said they share the "grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups", and added the US is the "leading donor for the Rohingya refugee humanitarian response".Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attaché be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.

schema.headline: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules

title: COP31: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
description: In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops
body: In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable."Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC."Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village."As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school."They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain."This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding."Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda."If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets."We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved.Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones."If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said.Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more.The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn.Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024.Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa.Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation.But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience?"If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam."Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited."Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support."The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued.She said this created a vicious cycle - countries lack support to prepare their plans, while not having the plans makes it harder to secure funding for climate resilience."When countries lack adequate adaptation planning and, more importantly, the resources to implement those plans, governments are forced into a cycle of responding to disasters instead of preventing or reducing their impacts," said Amos Wemanya, senior climate adviser at Power Shift Africa."Instead of investing in early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, water security and flood protection, scarce public resources are repeatedly diverted towards emergency relief and reconstruction. This costs more over time and leaves communities increasingly vulnerable."African negotiators acknowledge that adaptation plans help countries prioritise investments and attract funding, but argue that their absence should not be used to deny them financial support."Of course, having a comprehensive NAP helps countries prioritise investments and prepare proposals for climate finance," said Mahlet Eyassu Melkie, a senior strategic adviser to Ethiopia's COP32 presidency."But Africa's adaptation financing needs are based on scientific assessments, climate vulnerability, national priorities and regional estimates – not simply on whether every country has submitted a particular planning document."The UN Development Programme, which has helped more than 45 countries prepare their plans, said NAPs can help governments mobilise international support and coordinate climate action.Fred Njehu, a Pan-African political strategist at Greenpeace Africa, said their absence could nevertheless create significant obstacles."It is fair to acknowledge that missing adaptation plans act as a major functional barrier that severely bottlenecks the speed, volume and quality of international funding a country can access," he said.But having a plan does not guarantee the money needed to implement it."Even countries that have completed their NAPs have not received money anywhere near what they require for implementation of their adaptation plans," Apiny said.Kenya offers an example of how adaptation measures can help communities cope with climate pressures.In the country's arid and semi-arid south-east, concrete sand dams slow the flow of seasonal rivers, allowing sand to accumulate and store water underground. Communities can access it during dry periods using hand pumps or by scooping it out.UK charity Sand Dams Worldwide and its local partner, the Africa Sand Dam Foundation, said they had built about 1,300 such dams, improving access to water as droughts become more frequent and intense.But many vulnerable communities elsewhere on the continent are still waiting for similar interventions.Back in drought-hit Karamoja, Lobur wonders how different things might have been if farmers had access to small-scale irrigation schemes."We do have some underground water sources in some places. If there were proper plans and programmes, we could have tapped them to grow food, but we are having to live in hunger instead," Lobur said."My grandmother keeps reminding us how she lost eight children during a famine-like situation in 1982, and we all fear we might perish like that too."

title: California targets Nvidia in China AI chip probe
description: Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspec
body: Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating  Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.Huang has acknowledged engaging in extramarital affairs – and left the company last week after reports that he had relationships with subordinates.
